title: Kinematics in one dimension
description: Constant acceleration, free fall, displacement, and reading motion graphs. An example bank: see docs/bank-format.md for how to write your own.
author: Physics Quiz examples

questions.prompt: A ball is released from rest and falls freely for $1.00\,\mathrm{s}$. Taking $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and ignoring air resistance, what is its speed?

options.why: This is $\tfrac{1}{2}gt$, the **average** speed over the fall, not the speed at the end of it.
This is $2gt$. Check which factor the kinematic equation actually carries.
That is a distance, not a speed. Checking units is the fastest way to catch this one.

questions.explanation: From rest, $v = gt = 9.81 \times 1.00 = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The distance fallen in the same second is $\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 4.91\,\mathrm{m}$, which is why the other numbers look tempting.

questions.prompt: A car braking with constant deceleration stops in a distance $d$ from speed $v$. From speed $2v$, with the same deceleration, it stops in a distance of:

options.why: Stopping distance is not proportional to speed. Look at which power of $v$ appears in $v^2 = 2ad$.
Doubling the speed must increase the stopping distance; the kinetic energy to dissipate has grown.
This inverts the relationship: distance goes as the square of speed, not the square root.

questions.explanation: With $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2ad$ and a final speed of zero, $d = v_0^2 / (2a)$. Stopping distance goes as the **square** of the initial speed, so doubling the speed quadruples the distance. This is why speed limits matter more than they intuitively seem to.

questions.prompt: On a velocity against time graph, what does the area between the curve and the time axis represent?

options.why: Acceleration is the **slope** of a velocity against time graph, not its area.
Average velocity is the area divided by the elapsed time, not the area itself.
Jerk is the rate of change of acceleration, which on this graph would be the change in the slope.

questions.explanation: Velocity is the rate of change of position, so integrating velocity over time gives displacement: $\Delta x = \int v\,\mathrm{d}t$. Area below the axis counts as negative, which is exactly why area gives displacement rather than distance travelled.

questions.prompt: One ball is dropped from a height $h$ at the same instant an identical ball is fired horizontally from the same height. Ignoring air resistance, which lands first?

options.why: The horizontal motion does not slow the fall: the two motions are independent.
Moving horizontally gives no upward support, so it does not stay aloft any longer.

options.text: They land at the same time
It depends on the horizontal speed
options.why: Horizontal speed sets how far the ball travels, not how long it falls.

questions.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent under gravity. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and fall under the same $g$, so both take $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. The fired ball simply travels further sideways in that same time.

questions.prompt: A cyclist rides out at $10\,\mathrm{km/h}$ and returns along the same route at $20\,\mathrm{km/h}$. What is the average speed for the round trip?

options.why: This averages the speeds, but more time is spent at the slower speed, so the true average is lower.
The average **velocity** is zero for a round trip, but speed is distance over time and cannot be zero here.
Close, but check the arithmetic: the harmonic mean of 10 and 20 is $2(10)(20)/(10+20)$.

questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance over total time, not the mean of the speeds. For equal distances it is the harmonic mean: $\frac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2} = \frac{2(10)(20)}{30} = 13.3\,\mathrm{km/h}$. The slower leg takes twice as long, so it dominates.

questions.prompt: A car travelling at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ brakes with a constant deceleration of $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$. How long does it take to stop?

options.why: This is $a/v$, the ratio upside down. Its units are $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, not seconds, which gives it away.
That is the stopping **distance**, $v^2/2a$. The question asks for a time.
This multiplies speed by deceleration. The units come out as $\mathrm{m^2/s^3}$, so it cannot be a time.

questions.explanation: From $v = u + at$ with final speed $v = 0$: $t = u/|a| = 20 / 5.0 = 4.0\,\mathrm{s}$. The speed falls by $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ every second, and it has $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to lose.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up. Ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration at the highest point of its flight?

options.why: The **velocity** is zero at the top, for an instant. The acceleration is not: if it were, the ball would stay up there.
Nothing pushes the ball up once it has left the hand. The only force on it is its weight, which points down.

options.text: It depends on how hard the ball was thrown
options.why: The throw sets the starting velocity, and so how high the ball goes. Gravity sets the acceleration, and that is the same throughout.

questions.explanation: Once released, the only force on the ball is gravity, so its acceleration is $g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ downwards the whole time: on the way up, at the top and on the way down. At the top the velocity is changing from upwards to downwards, which is exactly what a downward acceleration does.

questions.prompt: On a graph of position against time, what does the gradient (slope) of the line represent?

options.why: Acceleration is the gradient of a **velocity**–time graph. On a position–time graph it shows up as curvature, not slope.
The vertical axis shows position. Distance travelled comes from how far that position changes, not from the slope.
Displacement is a change in the vertical coordinate. The gradient is that change **divided by** the time taken.

questions.explanation: The gradient is $\Delta x / \Delta t$, change in position over change in time, which is the definition of velocity. A steeper line means a faster object, and a line sloping down means motion in the negative direction.

questions.prompt: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ for $5.0\,\mathrm{s}$. How far does it travel in that time?

options.why: $at = 10$ is the car's final **speed**, in $\mathrm{m/s}$, not a distance.
This is $at^2$, missing the factor of one half. The car only reaches $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$ at the very end, so it covers less than $10 \times 5.0$.
This is $\tfrac{1}{2}at$: the time has to be squared.

questions.explanation: From rest, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2.0 \times 5.0^2 = 25\,\mathrm{m}$. As a check, the speed rises steadily from 0 to $10\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the average speed is $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, and $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s} \times 5.0\,\mathrm{s} = 25\,\mathrm{m}$.

questions.prompt: A runner completes exactly one lap of a $400\,\mathrm{m}$ track in $80\,\mathrm{s}$, finishing where they started. What is their average **velocity** over the lap?

options.why: That is the average **speed**: distance over time. Velocity uses displacement, and the runner ends where they began.
That is the distance run, and it has units of length, not of velocity.
This is time over distance, upside down: its units are $\mathrm{s/m}$.

questions.explanation: Average velocity is displacement divided by time. After one full lap the displacement is zero, so the average velocity is $0/80 = 0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, even though the average speed was $400/80 = 5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
